meta.title: Electrocution Hazards in Construction Part II: Employer Responsibilities
meta.description: Learn employer responsibilities for controlling construction electrocution hazards, including power lines, wiring systems, GFCI protection, AEGCP, tools, cords, guarding, and lockout/tagout.

electrical-hazards-review.title: Reviewing Electrical Hazards on Construction Sites
electrical-hazards-review.content: Construction sites may contain multiple electrical hazards. Workers may encounter overhead or underground power lines, energized wiring, damaged cords and tools, defective equipment, wet conditions, temporary power systems, and improperly guarded electrical panels. Electrical contact may cause shock, burns, arc flash injuries, fires, explosions, or fatal electrocution. Electrocution — fatal exposure to electrical energy — has been a leading cause of death in construction. Employer responsibilities under 29 CFR 1926 Subpart K include identifying hazards, training workers, controlling exposure, maintaining safe equipment, and ensuring workers know how to report unsafe electrical conditions.
keyPoints: Construction sites contain multiple electrical hazards including overhead lines, damaged cords, and temporary wiring.
Electrical contact can cause shock, burns, arc flash, fire, explosion, or fatal electrocution.
Electrocution is, by definition, a fatal electrical event.
Employers must identify hazards, train workers, and ensure safe electrical conditions on the jobsite.

power-line-employer-responsibilities.title: Power Line Hazards and Employer Responsibilities
power-line-employer-responsibilities.content: All overhead power lines must be treated as energized unless confirmed otherwise by the utility. The preferred protective method when work is performed near overhead power lines is to have the utility de-energize and visibly ground the lines before work begins. When lines cannot be de-energized, employers must maintain safe clearance distances and use appropriate protective controls such as insulating gloves, sleeves, blankets, hoods, matting, line hoses, and insulated hard hats. Employers must inform workers about jobs that involve power line hazards and ensure workers know whom to contact when they have questions. OSHA 1926.1408 requires employers to determine line voltage and minimum approach distances for equipment operations near energized lines.
keyPoints: Treat all overhead power lines as energized unless confirmed de-energized and grounded.
De-energizing and grounding lines is the preferred method when working near overhead power.
When lines cannot be de-energized, safe clearance distances and protective controls must be maintained.
Employers must inform workers of power line hazards and required safety measures.

wiring-outlets-cabinets.title: Controlling Wiring, Outlets, Cabinets, and Power Supplies
wiring-outlets-cabinets.content: Proper installation and maintenance of wiring systems, outlet boxes, cabinets, and power supplies is an employer responsibility under 29 CFR 1926 Subpart K. Wires entering boxes and cabinets must be protected from abrasion. Unused openings in cabinets, fittings, and breaker boxes must be closed to prevent accidental contact with energized parts. Circuit breaker boxes, pull boxes, and outlet boxes must have covers. Metal covers must be grounded. Outlet boxes in energized installations must have faceplates or fixture canopies. Flexible cord openings must have protective bushings or smooth rounded surfaces to prevent insulation damage.
keyPoints: Unused openings in cabinets and breaker boxes must be closed to prevent contact with energized parts.
All outlet boxes, pull boxes, and breaker panels must have proper covers.
Metal covers must be grounded.
Wires entering boxes must be protected from abrasion by bushings or smooth entry points.

gfci-grounding-protection.title: Ground-Fault Circuit Interrupters and Grounding Protection
gfci-grounding-protection.content: GFCIs protect workers from severe or fatal shock by interrupting electrical current when a ground fault is detected. GFCI protection is especially important in wet, damp, outdoor, or temporary power environments common on construction sites. GFCIs must never be bypassed, removed, or ignored. A GFCI that trips repeatedly during equipment use is a warning signal that the tool or cord may have a ground fault — the correct response is to stop work and report the problem, not to bypass the GFCI. Receptacles on extension cords must be protected. Workers must follow site procedures for testing GFCIs before use.
keyPoints: GFCIs interrupt current during a ground fault and protect workers from severe or fatal shock.
GFCIs must never be bypassed, removed, or ignored.
A repeatedly tripping GFCI signals a ground fault — stop work and report the problem.
GFCI protection is especially critical in wet, damp, or outdoor construction environments.

assured-equipment-grounding.title: Assured Equipment Grounding Conductor Programs
assured-equipment-grounding.content: An Assured Equipment Grounding Conductor Program (AEGCP) is an OSHA-recognized alternative to GFCI protection for ensuring grounding safety. It must be implemented by a competent person and include a written description of the program kept at the job site and accessible to employees and OSHA personnel. The program requires visual inspection of covered equipment before each day of use, continuity testing to verify grounding, testing of receptacles, plugs, and attachment caps for correct grounding connections, and removal from service of any damaged or defective equipment. Test records must be maintained until replaced by the next set of records.
keyPoints: An AEGCP is an alternative to GFCI protection and must be implemented by a competent person.
A written program description must be kept at the job site and available to workers and OSHA.
Equipment covered by the program must be visually inspected before each day of use.
Test records must be maintained and all damaged equipment removed from service.

tools-cords-maintenance.title: Maintaining Power Tools, Cords, and Electrical Equipment
tools-cords-maintenance.content: Employers must ensure electrical tools and cords are inspected before each use and maintained in safe condition. Workers must not use tools with damaged casings, exposed wires, loose plugs, or missing ground prongs. Removing a ground prong from a cord or tool is never acceptable — even if the tool continues to function. Exposed metal parts on equipment must be grounded. Electrical systems must maintain a continuous grounding path. Damaged equipment must be removed from service and repaired before reuse. Taping a damaged cord is not an acceptable repair. Where moisture exposure is possible, waterproof or sealable connectors should be used.
keyPoints: Inspect all tools and cords before every use for damage, missing ground prongs, or loose connections.
Never remove a ground prong — even if the tool operates normally without it.
Taping a damaged cord is not an acceptable repair — remove it from service.
Waterproof or sealable connectors should be used in areas with moisture exposure.

guarding-live-parts.title: Guarding Live Parts and Restricting Access
guarding-live-parts.content: Workers must be protected from accidental contact with energized parts. OSHA requires electrical equipment operating at 50 volts or more to be guarded to prevent such contact. Guarding may be achieved through enclosure, elevation, locked access, or physical barriers. Only authorized and qualified workers should access certain electrical equipment. Electrical rooms and panels must not be used for general storage — stored materials block access, create tripping hazards, and may expose workers to energized parts. Warning signs and controlled access help reinforce these protections.
keyPoints: Electrical equipment operating at 50 volts or more must be guarded against accidental contact.
Guarding may be achieved by enclosure, elevation, locked access, or physical barriers.
Only authorized and qualified workers should access electrical equipment areas.
Electrical rooms and panels must never be used for general tool or material storage.

lockout-tagout-electrical.title: Lockout/Tagout and Electrical Safety-Related Work Practices
lockout-tagout-electrical.content: Before servicing or maintaining electrically powered equipment, it must be de-energized through a proper lockout/tagout procedure. Turning a switch off alone is insufficient. Steps include identifying and de-energizing all energy sources including backup generators, applying locks and tags, verifying zero energy, and releasing stored energy. Lockout/tagout tags must clearly identify the equipment or circuit being worked on and the authorized employee performing the work. Only qualified persons may perform or verify work on energized electrical circuits when de-energization is not feasible. Workers must not re-energize equipment locked or tagged by another worker.
keyPoints: Turn off, lock out, tag out, and verify zero energy before servicing electrical equipment.
Lockout/tagout tags must identify the specific equipment and the authorized employee.
Never re-energize equipment locked or tagged by another worker.
Only qualified persons may work on energized circuits when de-energization is not feasible.

flexible-extension-cords.title: Flexible Cords, Extension Cords, and Jobsite Use
flexible-extension-cords.content: Extension cords on construction sites must be three-wire cords rated for hard or extra-hard usage. Two-wire household cords, cords with tape repairs, and cords not rated for construction use must not be used. Flexible cords must be protected from heat, oil, sharp edges, pinch points, moving equipment, and wet areas. Workers must not carry tools by their cords, yank cords from receptacles, route cords through doorways or windows where they could be pinched, or use indoor-only cords outdoors. Cords must be inspected before every use. Damaged cords must be removed from service immediately. Where moisture exposure is likely, use sealed or waterproof connectors.
keyPoints: Construction extension cords must be three-wire cords rated for hard or extra-hard usage.
Two-wire household cords and cords with tape repairs must not be used on construction sites.
Inspect cords before every use; remove damaged cords from service immediately.
Route cords to avoid heat, oil, sharp edges, pinch points, and wet surfaces.
